text:
Gray and damp to start this Sunday, with a mix of rain and wet snow flakes hanging on this morning before things dry out by mid afternoon. Don't expect much from it, barely a trace, though the European model and one other are more insistent on showers than the forecasters are. We stay cloudy with a high near 43, so it's a jacket day, but I'd still call the afternoon fair for a walk. Tonight stays cloudy and hovers right around freezing, so watch for a slick spot or two early Monday.

Monday is more of the same: stubborn clouds and a high near 44. Then the pattern flips. A big area of high pressure settles in and the sky finally clears out Tuesday, with highs near 50. From Wednesday on, we're in the 50s, maybe close to 60 in spots, and mostly dry. It'll feel more like mid-October than mid-November, so hold off on the heavy coat. Wear the jacket today, and plan the bigger outdoor stuff for midweek.

AFD KEY MESSAGES (forecaster's reasoning, issued 2026-11-15T07:06:00+00:00 — covers the whole BTV area, northern NY included: translate to what Burlington feels, never repeat other regions' place names):
  1. Lingering upslope snow showers gradually taper off today.
  2. A warm, dry and mostly sunny week is in store.
AFD WHAT CHANGED (same regional caveat): As of 206 AM EST Sunday... No significant changes.
AFD DISCUSSION (the forecaster's full reasoning, same regional caveat; their temps are area-wide ranges):
KEY MESSAGE 1: The moist cyclonic flow will continue through tonight, but the shortwave responsible for the widespread showers yesterday has passed to the south, ending most of the synoptic forcing. A subsidence inversion will form today and begin to lower, keeping the clouds trapped under it, but also decreasing the moisture depth. By tonight, the moisture depth should be too shallow to produce precipitation. Overall, only a couple tenths of an inch of additional snow accumulations are expected today. Tonight into Monday, the lowering inversion should drop below summit height and cause undercast to develop. KEY MESSAGE 2: A potent ridge and associated area of surface high pressure will dominate the weather this week, making it feel as if it were still mid-October. In a classic El Nino pattern, deep troughing and strong surface lows over the Pacific have caused continuous southwest to westerly flow out west, flooding the Great Plains and western Canada with warm Pacific air. This has caused temperature anomalies in the 20-30+ degree range. This airmass will begin to arrive Monday, but clouds will likely remain stuck under the inversion, so it will likely take until Tuesday to warm up. From then through the end of the week, and now likely through the weekend, highs in the 50s will prevail, though 60 will be possible in some of the warmest areas. There will be a strong, persistent subsidence inversion, and it will aided by the fact that significantly more surface heat will be lost at night than will be able to be replenished by the sun during the day. Radiational cooling will help lows drop into the 20s and 30s, around climatological normals. Weak troughs will gradually erode the ridge from the north, but it looks like it will take through next weekend for the ridge to get pushed to the south and east. Therefore, cooler conditions and chances for precipitation to return will likely not occur until the start of the following week.

WCAX METEOROLOGIST (regional station — Burlington relevance only, never their branding): BURLINGTON, Vt. (WCAX) - Mt. Mansfield received around 4 inches of snow today, marking the latest date to receive an inch of snow or greater. This breaks the previous record of November 9th, 1985. Valley showers and mountain snow showers will taper to scattered mountain flurries this evening, with the flurries continuing overnight. A general 1 to 4 inches of snow fell in the region today, mainly in the mountains, but little additional accumulation is expected tonight. Lows will range from the mid-20s to mid-30s. Sunday will be a quieter day with mostly cloudy skies and scattered valley sprinkles and mountain flurries, mainly during the morning. It will be touch on the blustery side, so dress warmly as highs will be in the upper 30s to low 40s. Otherwise, it will be a fair day for outdoor plans. The week will have a return to an extended period of dry and mild weather, similar to what we’ve had in October. Monday will be partly sunny with highs in the 40s. Tuesday through Thursday will have plenty of sunshine with highs mainly in the 50s. Some upper 50s are possible by Thursday, so any snow will melt through the week. A weak cold front may touch off an isolated shower on Friday, otherwise there’s the possibility for the dry stretch to continue into next weekend.
NBC5 METEOROLOGIST (2026-11-14T12:56:00Z — same caveat): Staying chilly Sunday, but drier with more sun south — Watch for slick spots and patchy black ice overnight, as it stays cloudy with lingering showers of rain and snow. It will be seasonably cold, with lows in the 20s and 30s. Sunday stays mostly cloudy and chilly, with highs in the low 40s. Expect a few lingering mixed showers in the morning, before turning drier in the afternoon. A few breaks of sun are likely, especially in southern Vermont. Clouds will be stubborn on Monday, though a few late-day breaks of sun are likely. Highs again reach the low 40s. Tuesday marks the transition toward brighter and warmer weather. Expect a mix of sun and clouds, with highs near 50. The Wednesday through Friday stretch looks beautiful, with partly sunny skies and highs reaching the mid to upper 50s. The mild and quiet pattern likely continues into the beginning of Thanksgiving week.
